item.title: Saijo Sake: Brewed with Ishizuchi's Water — Guide
item.description: Saijo, a city at the foot of Mount Ishizuchi in eastern Ehime, is celebrated as a town of water. Pure snowmelt and rainfall from the sacred mountain filter down through the ground and rise back up all over the city as ‘uchinuki’, free-flowing artesian spring water so clean and abundant that residents draw it for drinking and cooking from spouts around town. This exceptional soft water is the foundation of Saijo’s sake brewing: local breweries use it to produce clean, refined sake much prized in the region.

item.title: Tosa Sake: Kochi's Crisp Dry Rice Wine — Guide
item.description: Kochi, the old province of Tosa, is famous throughout Japan for its drinking culture, with a reputation for warm, open hospitality fuelled by generous quantities of sake. Tosa sake is characteristically crisp and dry — ‘karakuchi’ — made to complement the region’s fresh seafood rather than overpower it, and it pours freely at banquets, markets and izakaya across Kochi. Breweries such as Suigei (‘drunken whale’, a name that captures the local spirit) and other long-established kura produce well-regarded labels you can taste around the prefecture.

item.title: Nara Sake: The Birthplace of Refined Sake — Guide
item.description: Nara has a strong claim to be the birthplace of modern refined sake: it was in the temples of Nara, above all Shoryaku-ji, that the techniques for brewing clear, filtered sake (as opposed to cloudy doburoku) were perfected in the 15th century, in the style known as sobo-shu that shaped all Japanese sake that followed. The prefecture remains a distinguished brewing region, its historic kura clustered in Naramachi and towns across the Yamato plain, several producing celebrated labels.
